{{Short description|Solution of a simplified form of an equation}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''method of dominant balance''' approximates the solution to an equation
by solving a simplified form of the equation containing 2 or more of the equation's terms that most influence (dominate) the solution and excluding terms contributing only small modifications to this approximate solution.  Following an initial solution, [[iteration]] of the procedure may generate additional terms of an [[asymptotic expansion]] providing a more accurate solution.{{sfn|White|2010|p=2}}{{sfn|de Bruijn|1981|pp=187-189}}  

An early example of the dominant balance method is the [[Newton polygon]] method.  [[Isaac Newton|Newton]] developed this method to find an explicit approximation for an [[algebraic function]].  Newton expressed the function as proportional to the [[Dependent and independent variables|independent variable]] raised to a [[Exponentiation|power]], retained only the [[Degree of a polynomial|lowest-degree]] polynomial terms (dominant terms), and solved this simplified reduced equation to obtain an approximate solution.{{sfn|Christensen|1996}}{{sfn|White|2010|pp=1-14}} 
Dominant balance has a broad range of applications, solving [[differential equation]]s arising in [[fluid mechanics]], [[Plasma (physics)|plasma physics]], [[turbulence]], [[combustion]], [[nonlinear optics]], [[geophysical fluid dynamics]], and [[neuroscience]].{{sfn|Fishaleck|White|2008}}{{sfn|Callaham|Koch|Brunton|Kutz|2021}}

==Asymptotic relations==
The functions <math display="inline">f(z)</math> and <math>g(z)</math> of [[parameter]] or [[Dependent and independent variables|independent variable]] <math display="inline">z</math> and the quotient <math display="inline">f(z)/g(z)</math> have [[Limit (mathematics)|limits]] as <math display="inline">z</math> approaches the limit <math display="inline">L</math>.

The function <math display="inline">f(z)</math> is <em> much less than </em> <math display="inline">g(z) </math> as <math display="inline">z</math> approaches <math display="inline">L</math>, written as <math display="inline">f(z) \ll g(z) \ (z \to L)</math>, if  the limit of the quotient <math display="inline">f(z)/g(z)</math> is zero as <math display="inline">z</math> approaches <math display="inline">L</math>.{{sfn|Paulsen|2013|pp=1-3,7}}

The [[Relation (mathematics)|relation]] <math display="inline">f(z)</math> is <em>lower order</em> than <math display="inline">g(z)</math> as <math display="inline">z</math> approaches <math display="inline">L</math>, written using [[Big O notation|little-o]] notation <math display="inline">f(z)=o(g(z)) \ (z \to L)</math>, is identical to the <math display="inline">f(z)</math> is <em> much less than </em> <math display="inline">g(z) </math> as <math display="inline">z</math> approaches <math display="inline">L</math> relation.{{sfn|Paulsen|2013|pp=1-3,7}}

The function <math display="inline">f(z)</math> is <em>equivalent</em> to <math display="inline">g(z) </math> as <math display="inline">z</math> approaches <math display="inline">L</math>, written as <math display="inline">f(z) \sim g(z) \ (z \to L)</math>, if  the limit of the quotient <math display="inline">f(z)/g(z)</math> is 1 as <math display="inline">z</math> approaches <math display="inline">L</math>. {{sfn|Paulsen|2013|pp=1-3,7}}

This result indicates that the [[0|zero function]], <math display="inline">f(z)=0</math> for all values of <math display="inline">z</math>, can never be equivalent to any other function.{{sfn|Paulsen|2013|pp=1-3,7}}

Asymptotically equivalent functions remain asymptotically equivalent under [[Integral|integration]] if requirements related to convergence are met.  There are more specific requirements for asymptotically equivalent functions to remain asymptotically equivalent under [[Derivative|differentiation]].{{sfn|Olver|1974|pp=8,9,21}}

==Equation properties==
An equation's approximate solution is <math display="inline">s(z)</math> as <math display="inline">z</math> approaches limit <math display="inline">L</math>.  The equation's terms that may be constants or contain this solution are <math display="inline">T_{0}(s),T_{1}(s), \ldots, T_{n}(s)</math>.  If the approximate solution is fully correct, the equation's terms sum to zero in this equation:
<math display=block>T_{0}(s)+T_{1}(s)+ \ldots +T_{n}(s)=0.</math> 
For distinct [[integer]] indices <math display="inline">i,j</math>, this equation is a sum of 2 terms and a remainder <math display="inline">R_{ij}(s)</math> expressed as
<math display=block>\begin{align}
&T_{i}(s)+T_{j}(s)+ R_{ij}(s)=0 \\
&R_{ij}(s)=\sum^{n}_{{k=0} \atop {k \ne i, k \ne j}} T_{k}(s).
\end{align}
</math>

<em>Balance</em> equation terms <math display="inline">T_{i}(s)</math> and <math display="inline">T_{j}(s)</math> means find the function 
<math display="inline">s(z)</math> that solves the <em>reduced equation</em> <math display="inline">T_{i}(s)+T_{j}(s)=0</math> with <math display="inline">T_{i}(s) \ne 0</math> and <math display="inline">T_{j}(s) \ne 0</math>.{{sfn|Neu|2015|pp=2-4,14}}  This solution <math display="inline">s(z)</math> is <em>consistent</em> if terms <math display="inline">T_{i}(s)</math> and <math display="inline">T_{j}(s)</math> are <em>dominant</em>; dominant means the remaining equation terms <math display="inline">R_{ij}(s)</math> are much less than terms <math display="inline">T_{i}(s)</math> and <math display="inline">T_{j}(s)</math> as <math display="inline">z</math> approaches <math display="inline">L</math>.{{sfn|White|2010|pp=49-51}}{{sfn|Bender|Orszag|1999|pp=82-84}}  A consistent solution that balances two equation terms may generate an accurate approximation to the full equation's solution for <math display="inline"> z</math> values approaching <math display="inline">L</math>.{{sfn|Bender|Orszag|1999|pp=82-84}}{{sfn|Kruskal|1962|p=19}}  Approximate solutions arising from balancing different terms of an equation may generate distinct approximate solutions e.g. [[Method of matched asymptotic expansions|inner and outer layer solutions]].{{sfn|Fishaleck|White|2008}} 

In some cases, the reduced equation has coefficients containing a parameter <math display="inline">\epsilon</math>, but the parameter's exponent is different for the 2 terms.  In this case, the reduced equation requires a <em>scale transformation</em> <math display="inline">z=\epsilon^{\lambda} \tilde{z}</math> of the variable <math display="inline">z</math> using scaling exponent <math display="inline">\lambda</math>.  The dominant balance method selects a scaling exponent <math display="inline">\lambda</math> to generate transformed terms, each transformed term now containing the parameter with the same exponent.  Distinct pairs of terms and scaling transformations lead to distinct simplified equations called <em>distinguished limits</em>, and each equation may lead to a distinct solution.{{sfn|Neu|2015|pp=2-4,14}}{{sfn|Hinch|1991|p=62}}  The [[Newton polygon|Kruskal-Newton diagram]] facilitates identifying the required scale transformation needed for dominant balance of algebraic and differential equations.{{sfn|Fishaleck|White|2008}} 

For differential equation solutions containing an [[Regular singular point|irregular singularity]], the <em>leading behavior</em> is the first term of an asymptotic series solution that remains when the independent variable <math display="inline">z</math> approaches an irregular singularity <math display="inline">L</math>.  The <em>controlling factor</em> is the fastest changing part of the leading behavior.  It is advised to "show that the equation for the function obtained by factoring off the dominant balance solution from the exact solution itself has a solution that varies less rapidly than the dominant balance solution."{{sfn|Bender|Orszag|1999|pp=82-84}}

==Algorithm==
The input is the set of equation terms and the limit L.  The output is the set of approximate solutions. For each pair of distinct equation terms <math display="inline">T_{i}(s),T_{j}(s)</math> the algorithm applies a scale transformation if needed, balances the selected terms by finding a function that solves the reduced equation and then determines if this function is consistent.  If the function balances the terms and is consistent, the algorithm adds the function to the set of approximate solutions, otherwise the algorithm rejects the function.  The process is repeated for each pair of distinct equation terms.

:'''Inputs''' Set of equation terms <math display="inline">\{ T_{0}(s), T_{1}(s), \ldots, T_{n}(s)\}</math> and limit <math display="inline">L</math>
:'''Output''' Set of approximate solutions <math display="inline">\{ s_{0}(z), s_{1}(z), \dots \}</math>
:# For each pair of distinct equation terms <math display="inline">T_{i}(s),T_{j}(s)</math> do:
:## Apply a scale transformation if needed.
:## Solve the reduced equation: <math display="inline">T_{i}(s)+T_{j}(s)=0</math> with <math display="inline">T_{i}(s) \ne 0</math> and <math display="inline">T_{j}(s) \ne 0</math>. 
:## Verify consistency: <math display="inline">R_{ij}(s) \ll T_{i}(s) \ (z \to L)</math> and <math display="inline">R_{ij}(s) \ll T_{j}(s) \ (z \to L).</math>
:## If function <math display="inline">s(z)</math> is consistent and solves the reduced equation, add this function to the set of approximate solutions, otherwise reject the function.

==Improved accuracy==
The method may be iterated to generate additional terms of an [[asymptotic expansion]] to provide a more accurate solution.{{sfn|Bender|Orszag|1999|pp=82-84}}  [[Iterative method]]s such as the [[Newton's method|Newton-Raphson method]] may generate a more accurate solution.{{sfn|White|2010|pp=1-14}}  A [[Perturbation theory|perturbation series]], using the approximate solution as the first term, may also generate a more accurate solution.{{sfn|Fishaleck|White|2008}}
==Examples==
===Algebraic function===
The dominant balance method will generate an approximate solution for variable <math display="inline">s</math> in [[algebraic equation]] <math display="inline">1-16s+\epsilon s^{5}=0 </math> that depends on parameter <math display="inline">\epsilon</math>.  This example computes asymptotic values as <math display="inline">\epsilon</math> approaches zero because this example's goal is finding solutions for small <math display="inline">\epsilon</math> parameter values.  The function <math display="inline">s=s(\epsilon)</math> denotes how the equation's solution depends on the equation's parameter <math display="inline">\epsilon</math>.  The [[solution set]] is enumerated as <math display="inline">\{ s_{0}(\epsilon),s_{1}(\epsilon), s_{2}(\epsilon), s_{3}(\epsilon), s_{4}(\epsilon) \} </math>.{{sfn|Rozman|2020}}
====Input====
The set of equation terms is <math display="inline">\{ 1, -16s, \epsilon s^{5} \}</math> and asymptotic computations are as <math display="inline">\epsilon</math> approaches zero. 
====First term pair====
:# Select the terms <math display="inline">1</math> and <math display="inline">-16s</math>.
:# Rewriting the selected terms as <math display="inline">\epsilon^{0} 1</math> and <math display="inline">-\epsilon^{0} 16s</math>, the parameter's exponents are the same (0,0) for both terms so no scale transformation needed.
:# Solve the reduced equation: <math>1-16s=0, s(\epsilon)= \tfrac{1}{16}</math>. 
:# Verify consistency: <math>\epsilon s^{5} \ll 1 \ (\epsilon \to 0), \ \epsilon s^{5} \ll 16s \ (\epsilon \to 0) \ </math> for <math>s(\epsilon)=\tfrac{1}{16}.</math>  
:# Add this function  to the set of approximate solutions: <math>s_{0}(\epsilon)=\tfrac{1}{16}</math>. 
====Second term pair====
:# Select the terms <math>-16s</math> and <math>\epsilon s^{5}</math>.
:# Rewriting the selected terms as <math>-\epsilon^{0} 16s</math> and <math>\epsilon^{1} s^{5}</math>, the parameter's exponents are different (0,1) so a scale transformation is needed.  Apply the scale transformation <math>s=\epsilon^{-1/4} \tilde{s}</math>.  The parameter exponents of the transformed terms <math>- \epsilon^{-1/4} 16 \tilde{s}</math> and <math>\epsilon^{-1/4} \tilde{s}^{5}=0</math> are the same (-1/4,-1/4).  The transformed equation becomes <math>\epsilon^{1/4}-16 \tilde{s}+\tilde{s}^{5}=0</math>.
:# Solve the reduced equation: <math>-16 \tilde{s}+\tilde{s}^{5}=0, \ \tilde{s}= 2, -2, 2i, -2i </math>.
:# Verify consistency: <math>\epsilon^{1/4} \ll 16 \tilde{s} \ (\epsilon \to 0), \ \epsilon^{1/4} \ll \tilde{s}^{5} \ (\epsilon \to 0) \ </math> for <math>\tilde{s}= 2, -2, 2i, -2i.</math> 
:# Add these functions to the set of approximate solutions:
<math display=block>s_{1}(\epsilon)=\frac{2}{\epsilon^{1/4}},s_{2}(\epsilon)=\frac{-2}{\epsilon^{1/4}},s_{3}(\epsilon)=\frac{2i}{\epsilon^{1/4}},s_{4}(\epsilon)=\frac{-2i}{\epsilon^{1/4}}.</math>
====Third term pair====
:# Select the terms <math>1</math> and <math>\epsilon s^{5}</math>.
:# Rewriting the selected terms as <math>\epsilon^{0} 1</math> and <math>\epsilon^{1} s^{5}</math>, the parameter's exponents are different (0,1) so a scale transformation is needed. Apply the scale transformation <math>s=\epsilon^{-1/5} \tilde{s}</math>.  The parameter exponents of the transformed terms <math>\epsilon^{0} 1</math> and <math>\epsilon^{0} \tilde{s}^{5}</math> are the same (0,0).  The transformed equation is <math>1-16 \epsilon^{-1/5} \tilde{s}+\tilde{s}^{5}=0.</math>
:# Solve the reduced equation: <math>1+\tilde{s}^{5}=0, \ \tilde{s}= (-1)^{1/5}.</math>
:# The function is not consistent: <math>-16 \epsilon^{-1/5}\tilde{s} \gg 1 \ (\epsilon \to 0), \ \epsilon^{-1/5}\tilde{s} \gg \tilde{s}^{5} \ (\epsilon \to 0) \ </math> for <math>\tilde{s}= (-1)^{1/5}.</math>
:# Reject this function: <math>s= \epsilon^{-1/5} (-1)^{1/5}.</math>
====Output====
The set of approximate solutions has 5 functions:
<math display=block>
\left \{ 
\frac{1}{16}, 
\frac{2}{\epsilon^{1/4}}, 
\frac{-2}{\epsilon^{1/4}},
\frac{2i}{\epsilon^{1/4}},
\frac{-2i}{\epsilon^{1/4}} 
\right \}.</math>
====Perturbation series solution====
The approximate solutions are the first terms in the  perturbation series solutions.{{sfn|Rozman|2020}}
:<math display="block">
\begin{aligned}
& s_0(\epsilon)=\frac{1}{16}+\frac{1}{16777216} \epsilon^{1}+\frac{5}{17592186044416} \epsilon^{2}+\ldots, \\

& s_1(\epsilon)=\frac{2}{\epsilon^{1/4}}-\frac{1}{64} -\frac{5}{16384} \epsilon^{\frac{1}{4}}-\frac{5}{524288} \epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}-\ldots, \\

& s_2(\epsilon)=-\frac{2}{\epsilon^{1/4}}-\frac{1}{64}+\frac{5}{16384} \epsilon^{\frac{1}{4}}-\frac{5}{524288} \epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}+\ldots, \\

& s_3(\epsilon)=\frac{2i}{\epsilon^{1/4}}-\frac{1}{64} +\frac{5 i}{16384} \epsilon^{\frac{1}{4}}+\frac{5}{524288} \epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}-\ldots \\

& s_4(\epsilon)=-\frac{2i}{\epsilon^{1/4}}-\frac{1}{64} -\frac{5 i}{16384} \epsilon^{\frac{1}{4}}+\frac{5}{524288} \epsilon^{\frac{1}{2}}+\ldots, \\
\end{aligned}</math>

===Differential equation===
The differential equation <math display="inline">z^{3}w^{\prime \prime}-w=0</math> is known to have a solution with an exponential leading term.{{sfn|Olver|1974|pp=190-191}}  The transformation <math display="inline"> w(z)=e^{s(z)}</math> leads to the differential equation <math display="inline">1-z^{3}(s^{\prime})^{2}-z^{3}s^{\prime \prime}=0</math>.  The dominant balance method will find an approximate solution   as <math display="inline">z</math> approaches zero because this example's focus is for solutions for small <math display="inline">z</math> values.  Scaled transformations will not be used because there are  no equation parameters.  Two consecutive applications of the dominant balance method will generate the 2 leading terms of an asymptotic series.{{sfn|White|2010|pp=49-51}} 
====Input====
The set of equation terms is <math display="inline">\{ 1,-z^{3}(s^{\prime})^{2},-z^{3}s^{\prime \prime} \}</math> and the limit is zero. 
=====First term pair=====
:# Select <math>1</math> and <math>-z^{3}(s^{\prime})^{2}</math>.
:# The scale transformation is not required.
:#Solve the reduced equation: <math>1-z^{3}(s^{\prime})^{2}=0, \ s(z)=\pm 2z^{-1/2}</math>
:# Verify consistency: <math>z^{3}s^{\prime \prime} \ll 1 \ (z \to 0), \ z^{3}s^{\prime \prime} \ll z^{3}(s^{\prime})^{2} \ (z \to 0)</math> for <math> s(z)=\pm 2z^{-1/2}.</math>
:# Add these 2 functions to the set of approximate solutions: <math>s_{+}(z)= +2z^{-1/2}, \ s_{-}(z)= -2z^{-1/2}.</math>
====Second term pair====
:# Select <math>1</math> and <math>-z^{3}s^{\prime \prime}</math>
:# The scale transformation is not required.
:# Solve the reduced equation: <math>1-z^{3}s^{\prime \prime}=0, \ s(z)=\tfrac{1}{2}z^{-1}</math> 
:# The function is not consistent: <math>z^{3}(s^{\prime})^{2} \gg 1 \ (z \to 0), \ z^{3}(s^{\prime})^{2} \gg  z^{3}s^{\prime \prime} \ (z \to 0)</math> for <math>s(z)=\tfrac{1}{2}z^{-1}.</math>
:# Reject this function: <math>s(z)=\tfrac{1}{2}z^{-1}.</math>.
====Third term pair====
:# Select <math>-z^{3}(s^{\prime})^{2}</math> and <math>-z^{3}s^{\prime \prime}</math>.
:# The scale transformation is not required. 
:# Solve the reduced equation: <math>z^{3}(s^{\prime})^{2}+z^{3}s^{\prime \prime}=0, \ s(z)=\ln z</math>.
:# The function is not consistent: <math>1 \gg z^{3}(s^{\prime})^{2} \ (z \to 0) \ </math> and <math>\ 1 \gg  \ z^{3}s^{\prime \prime} \ (z \to 0)</math> for <math>s(z)=\ln z.</math> 
:# Reject this function: <math>s(z)=\ln z.</math>
====Output====
The set of approximate solutions has 2 functions:{{sfn|White|2010|pp=49-51}}
<math display=block>
\left \{ +2z^{-1/2}, -2z^{-1/2} \right \}.</math>

====Find 2-term solutions====
Using the 1-term solution, a 2-term solution is
<math display=block>s_{2\pm}(z)=\pm 2z^{-1/2}+s(z).</math>
Substitution of this 2-term solution into the original differential equation generates a new differential equation:{{sfn|White|2010|pp=49-51}}
<math display=block>
\begin{align}
1-z^{3}(s_{2\pm}^{\prime})^{2}-z^{3}s_{2\pm}^{\prime \prime}&=0 \\
\pm 1 \mp \frac{4}{3}zs^{\prime}+\frac{2}{3} z^{5/2}(s^{\prime})^{2}+\frac{2}{3}z^{5/2}s^{\prime\prime}&=0.
\end{align}
</math>

====Input====
The set of equation terms is <math display="inline">\{  
\pm1, \mp \frac{4}{3}zs^{\prime}, \frac{2}{3} z^{5/2}(s^{\prime})^{2}, \frac{2}{3}z^{5/2}s^{\prime\prime} \}</math>  and the limit is zero.
=====First term pair=====
:1. Select <math>1</math> and <math>-\tfrac{4}{3}zs^{\prime}</math>.
:2. The scale transformation is not required.
:3. Solve the reduced equation: <math>1-\tfrac{4}{3}zs^{\prime}=0, \ s(z)=\tfrac{3}{4} \ln z</math>.
:4. Verify consistency: 
:<math> 
\tfrac{2}{3} z^{5/2}(s^{\prime})^{2}+\tfrac{2}{3}z^{5/2}s^{\prime\prime} \ll 1 \ (z \to 0), \text{for} \ s(z)=\tfrac{3}{4} \ln z </math> 
:<math> \tfrac{2}{3} z^{5/2}(s^{\prime})^{2}+\tfrac{2}{3}z^{5/2}s^{\prime\prime} \ll \tfrac{4}{3}zs^{\prime} \ (z \to 0) \ \text{for} \ s(z)=\tfrac{3}{4} \ln z.</math> 
:5. Add these functions to the set of approximate solutions: 
:<math display="inline">s_{2+}(z)=+ 2z^{-1/2}+\tfrac{3}{4} \ln z </math>
:<math display="inline">s_{2-}(z)=- 2z^{-1/2}+\tfrac{3}{4} \ln z</math>.{{sfn|White|2010|pp=49-51}}

====Other term pairs====
For other term pairs, the functions that solve the reduced equations are not consistent.{{sfn|White|2010|pp=49-51}}
====Output====
The set of approximate solutions has 2 functions:{{sfn|White|2010|pp=49-51}}
<math display=block>
\left \{ +2z^{-1/2}+\tfrac{3}{4} \ln z, -2z^{-1/2}+\tfrac{3}{4} \ln z \right \}.</math>

====Asymptotic expansion====
The next iteration generates a 3-term solution <math display="inline">s_{3 \pm}(z)=\pm 2z^{-1/2}+\tfrac{3}{4} \operatorname{ln}(z)+h(z)</math> with <math display="inline">h(z) \ll 1 \ (z \to 0)</math> and this means that a [[power series]] expansion can represent the remainder of the solution.{{sfn|White|2010|pp=49-51}}   
The dominant balance method generates the leading term to this asymptotic expansion with constant <math display="inline">A</math> and expansion coefficients determined by substitution into the full differential equation:{{sfn|White|2010|pp=49-51}} 
:<math>w(z)=A z^{3/4}e^{\pm 2z^{-1/2}} \left( \sum^{m}_{n=0} \ a_{n} z^{n/2} \right) </math> 
: <math>a_{n+1}=\pm \frac{(n-1/2)(n+3/2)a_{n}}{4(n+1)}.</math>
A partial sum of this non-convergent series generates an approximate solution.  The leading term corresponds to the [[WKB approximation|Liouville-Green (LG)]] or [[WKB approximation|Wentzel–Kramers–Brillouin (WKB)]] approximation.{{sfn|Olver|1974|pp=190-191}}
